name: Omar Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell or campaign for a side. Everything here is confidential. What did you work on this morning?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Omar Abbott, fifty-eight, and I prepare fishing co-op accounts and tax-return drafts at an accounting firm. I matched ice invoices to a landing sheet today; I like finding which boat actually bought the ice, and I dislike a missing skipper signature at filing time. I'm still junior and below our experienced reviewers' skill. I earned a bachelor's degree in accounting after years scheduling ferry crews.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do tools and home life shape the day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I use AI every day to group invoices, with a senior checking my work before it goes out. Maya teaches adult literacy, our children are grown and live separately, and our flat is paid off. The firm pays even its junior band well, we have fourteen months of expenses saved and plenty of other accounting firms nearby. I try a useful tool early, but I still need an actual payslip and a pension statement before making retirement plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fishing co-op accounts would still come in after each landing. I use AI every day to group fuel and ice invoices, then compare its list with the skipper's receipts before the senior signs a return.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team the grouping tool saves typing, not our responsibility for the figures. I'd ask the co-op treasurer to keep sending the original landing sheets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm fifty-eight and still a junior accountant; my bachelor's degree in accounting did not make me the strongest reviewer overnight. The firm pays its junior band well, and Maya and I have fourteen months of expenses saved. Our flat is paid off and there are plenty of other accounting firms near the port, so I feel secure in a modest-AI world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep preparing co-op accounts and tax drafts with the AI grouping I already use, under senior sign-off. This month I'd put the landing-sheet mismatches into a shared log so the senior can teach me which adjustments belong in the return. I'd keep our regular savings transfer and repair the kitchen tap from the household budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. The tool makes my pile neater, but the skipper's wet paper still needs a look.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did you get into this accounting job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maya teaches adult literacy classes and our two children have their own homes. I came into accounting after years scheduling ferry crews, so I know how the port sounds in a storm, but I am learning tax. I like reconciling a fuel slip to the right boat and dislike a missing signature after a long day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the mismatch log contain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shared log would use only the co-op's approved figures. I would ask the senior to check each adjustment until I can explain it back. A neat AI list is not a reason to skip that conversation.

I would keep **senior sign-off** on co-op returns.
think: Our **fourteen-month reserve** and paid-off flat give breathing room.
My **junior skill** still needs a senior’s careful review.
do: Continue **co-op returns** with existing AI grouping and senior checks.
Log **landing-sheet mismatches** this month for paid review.
feel: I feel **calm** about our present work and money.

fieldNote: His **high junior pay** comes from the firm’s pay band, not senior status or strong accounting skill.

steps.text: Keep preparing co-op returns with existing AI grouping and senior sign-off
Log landing-sheet mismatches for senior review this month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI writes whole returns and replies to clients, my invoice grouping could be folded into the system. I might lose paid hours before I have mastered the tax side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the partners to show the new rota and measured error rate. I'd say a boat owner still needs an answer when the fuel slip and landing sheet disagree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A cut to my own hours would matter even with savings, because Maya's teaching wage and our reserve are for ordinary life, not endless wage replacement. We have no mortgage, and several firms hire nearby, so I could search without panic. I use AI daily, but that does not grant me a protected post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build a new AI-assisted exception list from approved landing sheets during paid work time, with the senior checking the first ten cases. I'd ask the partner to approve a paid hour each week for testing it and keep my current rota while offered. If my hours are cut, I'd apply to posted paid accounts jobs only with written pay covering our regular bills, a signed start and ferry hours that fit Maya's confirmed evening classes; if none fits, I'd keep any paid firm work still offered and search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible loss of my own paid hours, though our reserve gives time. I won't confuse a clever exception list with a wage contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which error would the list catch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I once sent a fuel charge to the wrong boat because two skippers share a surname. The exception list could flag duplicate names before I post the entry. The senior would still decide whether the charge belongs in the return.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would a new rota affect evenings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maya teaches Tuesday and Thursday evenings, and I usually cook then. A new firm requiring late ferry travel would change that, so I would check its actual hours before signing. A posted vacancy without pay and a start is just an advert.

I would keep a **human answer** for disputed fuel slips.
think: My **junior hours** could shrink as AI expands.
Our **strong reserve** buys search time, not a protected wage.

Seek a **paid weekly hour** for the trial.

feel: I feel **anxious** about possible own-pay loss.

steps.text: Test new AI exception list on paid time with ten senior-checked cases and approved weekly hour

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2028 could prepare and check the accounts and returns that make up my desk week. Robots around 2031 come later, but I do not need a robot to lose an accounting wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the firm to put paid notice and remaining work in writing. I'd tell Maya we can use our reserve to search carefully, not treat it as a pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my junior desk post might end in the first year after 2028. Fourteen months saved and no mortgage give us a genuine runway, but Maya and I still need income for bills and future years. Nearby accounting firms could be cutting similar posts, so I would not count their signs as openings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd request a written pension forecast showing payment dates and amounts, without assuming any entitlement. I'd keep my paid co-op files and check posted ferry operations vacancies each month, drawing on my earlier crew-scheduling experience. If the firm ends my post in the first year after AGI arrives in 2028, I'd take a funded ferry role only with written pay covering our bills, a signed start and a rota fitting Maya's confirmed classes; if none fits, I'd keep any paid firm hours offered and use our reserve within a monthly spending cap while searching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious rather than overwhelmed. Fourteen months lets us choose a paid next step, but it is not a wage for the rest of my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would grown children support the household?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maya and I would show our grown children the budget if they asked, but not ask them to fund it. We would set a monthly limit on reserve withdrawals before my last payslip. A pension forecast may show a later payment; I would not spend it now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ferry work really be safer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ferry office might be hiring, but its scheduling desk is thinking work and faces AGI too. I would ask whether a posted role includes paid on-board safety checks, and I would not take it without written hours and wage. The robots in 2031 could reach more of that hands-on part.

say: I would ask for **written paid notice** and real openings.
I would treat the **reserve as search time**, not retirement income.
think: My **junior desk post** may end in the first year after 2028.
Our **fourteen-month reserve** cannot replace a lifelong wage.

After **2028 post loss**, take funded work only with written bills pay, signed start and fitting rota.
feel: I feel **anxious** while planning for possible loss.
S2.quote: Fourteen months lets us choose a paid next step, but it is not a wage for the rest of my life.
fieldNote: **Thinking AI** reaches both account work and ferry scheduling in 2028; only physical checks might last until robots around 2031.
The **ferry move** needs posted funding, written bill-covering pay, signed start and rota fitting Maya’s classes; reserve withdrawals have a cap.

steps.text: Request pension forecast and set monthly reserve withdrawal cap before post loss
Check posted funded ferry roles monthly; move after loss with written bills pay, signed start, rota
Keep offered paid co-op hours while no suitable funded post opens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years would let me test a ferry safety role without betting our flat on a new certificate. AGI in 2031 still takes the accounts desk and ferry scheduling; robots around 2034 might then reach on-board checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the ferry operator I have crew-scheduling experience but need a fresh safety credential. I'd tell my firm I would train on my own evenings if the fee and timetable really fit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I enjoy learning quickly, but I have not checked a vessel's safety equipment for years. Our fourteen-month reserve lets me pay a modest course fee without skipping bills. A certificate still does not guarantee a vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter I'd check the advertised fee and class dates for a ferry safety refresher, then enrol next spring if the fee stays below three hundred and evening classes do not cut my paid accounting hours. I'd complete the supervised practical check before applying for any on-board role. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, if my tax post ends, I'd take a posted funded ferry safety job only with written bills-covering pay, signed start and a rota fitting Maya's classes; if none opens, I'd keep any paid firm work offered and cap reserve withdrawals while searching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the desk but glad I can pay for a course without borrowing. I want a job offer, not just a certificate in a drawer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the course worth paying for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the course provider to show the exact fee, practical supervisor and dates. If the fee rises beyond our cap, I will not enrol and will keep the current paid work. I can look at another approved course later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the on-board work last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The on-board safety check still needs a person at the life rings today, but I won't assume that lasts beyond the later robots. I would ask the operator for a posted paid opening before I change jobs. Maya's evenings still decide which shifts fit.

I would ask for **real paid openings** before moving.

Complete a **supervised safety check** before applying.

S3.quote: I want a job offer, not just a certificate in a drawer.
fieldNote: Unlike a thin-cushion worker, he can **self-fund** a capped course on evenings without reducing paid accounting hours.
The **ferry path** requires a supervised practical, posted funded vacancy, written bills pay, signed start and Maya-compatible rota.

steps.text: Enrol in ferry safety refresher only below three hundred with evening classes preserving pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years puts me at sixty-eight, which might be a retirement date only if a real payment covers our bills. AGI in 2036 still ends most accounting preparation before robots arrive around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the firm for a dated transition plan and the ferry operator for written wages. I'd tell our grown children to make their own plans rather than count on our savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our flat is paid off and fourteen months saved gives us options, but I have not seen a pension amount or start date. I could keep working in a ferry role if the payments are inadequate. I would not leave paid work merely because a calendar says sixty-eight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Each January I'd check the pension statement's payable amount against our bills while keeping any paid firm hours offered. I'd enrol in the ferry safety refresher only if the fee stays under three hundred, the practical is supervised and evening classes preserve my wages. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, if my tax post ends and pension income is insufficient or not payable, I'd take a posted funded ferry role only with written bill-covering pay, signed start and a rota fitting Maya's classes; if no suitable role exists, I'd keep offered paid firm work and limit reserve withdrawals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about a future desk loss, but our current wage, paid-off flat and reserve make the long runway useful. I still need a payable pension number before changing work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would grown children help later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maya and I would review the statement together, not ask our grown son or daughter for money. If the payment is enough, we can decide separately whether to stop work then. If it is not, we will keep looking at paid roles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the pension covers your bills?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ferry course could be unnecessary if the pension really covers us in 2036, but I would rather test it while employed. A posted job with a signed start is different from a friendly invitation to visit a boat. I can afford to wait for the written terms.

S4.quote: I still need a payable pension number before changing work.
fieldNote: At **sixty-eight in 2036**, retirement depends on a verified payable amount covering bills, not age alone.
The **course** is self-funded only under a fee cap and without wage loss; post-loss ferry work needs funded written terms.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my junior accounting desk could vanish before a ferry safety route is ready. Fourteen months saved and a paid-off flat give us time, not a lifelong wage. Written notice, posted funded work and a signed start would help. A reserve is a runway, not a port to live in.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks a boat's physical safety kit while software prepares the co-op return. I could learn that work again, but a supervised practical and a paid vacancy have to exist. I would not trade a payslip for a memory of working at sea.

headlineQuote: A reserve is a runway, not a port to live in.
portrait: At **fifty-eight**, Omar drafts fishing co-op accounts and tax returns as a junior.
His **accounting bachelor’s** accompanies below-average accounting skill despite prior ferry scheduling experience.
He uses **AI daily** for invoice grouping while a senior signs his work.
Maya’s **teaching wage**, grown children, paid-off flat and fourteen-month reserve give choices.
His **higher junior pay** and many nearby firms permit a capped self-funded safety course.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his accounting desk before an alternative ferry role is ready.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **written notice**, posted funded work and a signed start.
